children: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has put 900 gigawatts (GW) of non-fossil power capacity by 2035, mostly solar and wind, firmly on India’s clean-energy agenda. The ambition is reflected in transmission investment plans for the next decade.

This raises three questions. First, how can these goals address power shortages and expensive power purchases by utilities? It is worth noting that, at present, 40 GW of low cost solar projects are unable to sell their power to discoms. Resolving this mismatch is essential to finding buyers for 900 GW.
Second, can a system dominated by solar and wind, as would be the case with a 900-GW goal, deliver reliable electricity at lower cost?
Third, will the transition strengthen India’s energy security and industry, or create new dependencies on imported technologies and critical materials?

The first puzzle is striking because deployment is accelerating. Industrial and commercial consumers buying electricity directly drive substantial growth: around 8 GW of open-access solar came online in 2025. Yet about 40 GW of auctioned projects remain without buyers.

The explanation lies partly in electricity’s changing value across the day, compounded by utilities’ procurement obligations and financial constraints. Solar-rich afternoons bring abundant cheap power, sometimes at near-zero exchange prices. After sunset, Indian Energy Exchange prices have repeatedly touched ₹10 per unit, with Tamil Nadu paying up to ₹37, while some States have faced shortages.
Addressing the mismatch

Two solutions address this mismatch. Dramatically cheaper battery storage makes daytime solar a cost-effective option for evening and nighttime demand. Batteries can be deployed in one to two years, compared with over five for conventional power, helping utilities address peak shortages and expensive purchases.

Second, significantly lower daytime tariffs can encourage demand to shift to solar hours. This already happens, but modestly. Cheap daytime electricity could replace expensive imported gas for industrial heating, relieving industry while creating buyers for unsold solar. Solarising agricultural feeders through PM-KUSUM also creates daytime demand and improves farmers’ electricity supply.

What about reliability and costs? Low-cost batteries again change the economics. SECI’s 1,000-MW “thermal-mimic” auction contracted a coal-like supply profile from renewables and storage, including high availability outside solar hours, at ₹5.25-5.26 per unit, fixed for 25 years. Adjusting for inflation, this is roughly ₹3.8 per unit. This benchmark for reliable, near-round-the-clock electricity, insulated from fuel-price escalation, demonstrates that renewables and storage can provide comparable reliability at substantially lower costs than conventional power.

Our analysis suggests around 200 GW of storage, transmission expansion and flexible demand could be critical for reliability and integrating 900 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2035. Existing and under-construction thermal plants remain important. This need not entail decades of expensive new coal power plant contracts. We estimate a least-cost clean-power pathway could cut average procurement costs by around 15 per cent in real terms, saving over ₹2 lakh crore annually by 2035.

The third question presents a challenge and opportunity. Affordable electricity can electrify transport and industrial heat, enable hydrogen production and strengthen industry. Imported oil and gas require repeated purchases; solar plants, batteries and grids deliver services for decades. Imported battery cells, critical minerals and technologies too create vulnerabilities requiring proactive action, building on domestic solar manufacturing progress.

Battery cells, for which India is dependent on imports, need not, however, implying importing most of its economic value. Pack assembly, power electronics, energy management, engineering, construction and operations can happen domestically. Domestic financing and ownership retain substantial long-term financial returns.

Depending on project economics, over 70 per cent of lifetime economic value could potentially remain domestic, even with imported cells. Affordability need not await complete self-reliance, while domestic battery manufacturing capacity is being built up. India’s Electricity Act, open access, captive and group-captive generation, auctions and exchanges provide institutional foundations.
Action plan
Five actions are needed to make the 900 GW clean power goal materialise and deliver benefits.

First, favour cheaper, faster renewables and storage over expensive, delayed coal projects. Before signing 25-30-year coal contracts, utilities should assess renewables, storage, demand flexibility and existing capacity against identical reliability requirements. New thermal plants should not be the default. Further, procure electricity services, not technologies. Specify peak-hour supply, availability and reliability. Technology-neutral auctions such as SECI’s thermal-mimic tender can discover the lowest-cost mix.

Second, ease grid connections for clean power projects by leveraging existing grid infrastructure. Implement and expand the ongoing programme allowing solar and storage projects to use existing solar projects’ underutilised grid access during nighttime hours.

Third, let consumer prices reflect the cost of supply, offering deep discounts during solar hours when electricity is cheap and solar generation is abundant. Consumers shifting pumping, cooling, charging or production to cheaper hours should retain the savings; peak consumption should face its true cost.

Fourth, let consumers choose suppliers. Large consumers should, by default, procure their own power to seek the best deals, as proposed in amendments to the Electricity Act. Incumbent utilities can remain suppliers of last resort, with explicitly funded subsidies.

Fifth, combine smart imports, domestic manufacturing and recycling. Import battery cells while building packs, controls and software domestically. Establish recycling capacity to recover critical materials from imported batteries, and expand domestic manufacturing to reduce supply-chain risks.

These reforms can unlock projects awaiting buyers, improve reliability, lower costs and strengthen industrial capabilities, delivering substantial benefits from India’s new 900-GW clean power goal for 2035.
Abhyankar and Phadke are Faculty Directors at the India Energy and Climate Center, UC Berkeley’s Goldman School

title: The potential of India’s clean power ambition
